own_scenes.desc: La estructura del techno clásico la renovaron las fusiones con el jazz, grupos con raíces en el electro (The Black Dog, Plaid, 808 State) y jóvenes estadounidenses formados en Atkins, May y Craig, como Dan Curtin, Morgan Geist o Titonton Duvante. El paralelo con el bebop es claro: música afroamericana resistida en casa, aceptada en Europa y popularizada por blancos. De UR al GFQ de Gregory Watts, Carl Craig (Innerzone Orchestra, con el contrabajista Rodney Whitaker y el percusionista Francisco Mora) y Kirk DeGiorgio llevaron músicos al estudio; Conjoint de David Moufang, Spacetime Continuum de Jonah Sharp, Velocette o los compases de 3/4 de Desert Scores de Ian O’Brien mostraron que la tecnología da al techno la libertad que el bebop dio al jazz. Acid Brass, en cambio, probó que «Strings of Life» sin la 909 de May se vuelve repetitiva.

refs.q: Jazz is one music genre from which techno seems to take all kinds of cues, and in fact the cultural parallels between techno and bebop in particular are striking: both originated with African American artists, both faced early resistance from U.S. audiences and traveled to Europe for greater acceptance, and both became popularized (some might say watered down) by white artists.
refs.para: Efforts to expand the structure of techno are also producing myriad combinations with jazz music. Jazz is one music genre from which techno seems to take all kinds of cues, and in fact the cultural parallels between techno and bebop in particular are striking: both originated with African American artists, both faced early resistance from U.S. audiences and traveled to Europe for greater acceptance, and both became popularized (some might say watered down) by white artists.
refs.chapter: Cap. 7: Beyond the Dance: The Future Sound of Techno, 1999–?

refs.q: These artists seem to sense that technology gives techno the same kind of freedom that bebop brought to jazz in the 1950s.
refs.para: While all of these jazz-related projects are ambitious, the most impressive still seem to be coming from studio-born projects, such as David Moufang’s loose collaboration Conjoint, all of Jonah Sharp’s work with Spacetime Continuum, and experiments with 3/4 time signatures in the work of Jason (Velocette) Williams and on Ian O’Brien’s Desert Scores. These artists seem to sense that technology gives techno the same kind of freedom that bebop brought to jazz in the 1950s.
